editorial.headline: Independent Athletes, and Bali’s PMA Boundary
editorial.standfirst: Independent athletes, including individual e-sports competitors, are nationally open to full foreign ownership—but a PT PMA cannot register the activity in Bali today.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register KBLI 93197 in Bali today through a PT PMA. That is the practical starting point, even though the activity is nationally open to foreign investment. The activity concerns sportspersons or athletes acting in their own individual capacity, expressly including individual e-sports participants. The wording places the person at the centre: it captures sporting activity carried on in the athlete’s personal capacity. It is a classification built around the independent athlete’s own professional activity—personal, direct and individual in form.

At the registration level, the activity is open to Mikro, Kecil and Menengah scales. These are the only scales given in the record. That matters because Bali’s recorded structural reason turns on what is absent: OSS has no Usaha Besar scale row for this activity. Bali consequently treats it as reserved for UMKM. For founders, that detail is more useful than a broad label: the permitted scale determines whether the activity can be recorded through a particular corporate form.

Across Indonesia, PMA is classified TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In ordinary language, the record makes room for full foreign ownership at national level; it does not impose a reduced foreign stake for this activity. There is no lower foreign ceiling to account for in this national entry. The source identified for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For an independent athlete considering the activity outside Bali, the national reading is therefore straightforward: the ownership ceiling itself does not close the door.

Bali changes the answer entirely. A PT PMA is Usaha Besar by law, and because no Usaha Besar row exists, it cannot register this activity there. The local status is Closed to PMA (no Besar scale): closed to PMA for the absence of a large-scale pathway, not because the national 100% ceiling has vanished. Bali also records a permanent, island-wide moratorium that blocks PMA registrations across the Low and Medium-Low risk band, under the Governor’s letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. The entry’s direct Bali conclusion remains unambiguous: national openness does not provide a PT PMA a registration route for this activity in Bali.
